{{More citations needed|date=September 2021}}
'''Buchholz's psi-functions''' are a hierarchy of single-argument [[Ordinal notation|ordinal functions]] <math>\psi_\nu(\alpha)</math> introduced by German mathematician Wilfried Buchholz in 1986. These functions are a simplified version of the <math>\theta</math>-functions, but nevertheless have the same strength{{huh|date=December 2020}} as those. Later on this approach was extended by Jäger<ref>{{cite journal|first=G|last=Jäger|title= ρ-inaccessible ordinals, collapsing functions and a recursive notation system|journal= [[Archiv für Mathematische Logik und Grundlagenforschung]]| volume = 24| issue = 1| date =1984| pages = 49–62|doi=10.1007/BF02007140|s2cid=38619369}}</ref> and [[Kurt_Schütte|Schütte]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=W.|last1=Buchholz| last2 = Schütte| first2 = K.| title = Ein Ordinalzahlensystem ftir die beweistheoretische Abgrenzung der H~-Separation und Bar-Induktion|journal=Sitzungsberichte der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Math.-Naturw. Klasse| date = 1983}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Buchholz defined his functions as follows. Define:
*&Omega;<sub>&xi;</sub> = &omega;<sub>&xi;</sub> if &xi; > 0, &Omega;<sub>0</sub> = 1
The functions &psi;<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') for ''&alpha;'' an ordinal, ''v'' an ordinal at most &omega;, are defined by induction on ''&alpha;'' as follows: 
*&psi;<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') is the smallest ordinal not in ''C''<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'')
where ''C''<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') is the smallest set such that 
*''C''<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') contains all ordinals less than &Omega;<sub>''v''</sub> 
*''C''<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') is closed under ordinal addition
*''C''<sub>''v''</sub>(''&alpha;'') is closed under the functions &psi;<sub>''u''</sub> (for ''u''&le;&omega;) applied to arguments less than &alpha;.

The limit of this notation is the [[Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal]].

== Properties ==

Let <math>P</math> be the class of [[additively principal]] ordinals. Buchholz showed following properties of this functions:

* <math>\psi_\nu(0)=\Omega_\nu, </math> <ref name="buchholz84">{{Cite journal |last=Buchholz |first=W. |date=1986 |title=A new system of proof-theoretic ordinal functions |journal=[[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]] |language=en |volume=32 |pages=195–207 |doi=10.1016/0168-0072(86)90052-7|doi-access=free |url=https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/3841/1/3841.pdf }}</ref>{{rp|p=197}}
* <math>\psi_\nu(\alpha)\in P, </math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=197}}
* <math>\psi_\nu(\alpha+1) = \min\{\gamma\in P: \psi_\nu(\alpha)<\gamma\}\text{ if } \alpha\in C_\nu(\alpha),</math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=199}}
* <math>\Omega_\nu\le\psi_\nu(\alpha)<\Omega_{\nu+1} </math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=197}}
* <math>\psi_0(\alpha)=\omega^\alpha \text{ if }\alpha<\varepsilon_0,</math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=199}}
* <math>\psi_\nu(\alpha)=\omega^{\Omega_\nu+\alpha} \text{ if } \alpha<\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1} \text{ and } \nu\neq 0,</math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=199}}
* <math>\theta(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1},0)=\psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1}) \text{ for } 0<\nu\le\omega.</math> <ref name="buchholz84" />{{rp|p=206}}

== Fundamental sequences and normal form for Buchholz's function ==

=== Normal form ===

The normal form for 0 is 0. If <math>\alpha</math> is a nonzero ordinal number <math>\alpha<\Omega_\omega</math> then the normal form for <math>\alpha</math> is <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu_1}(\beta_1)+\psi_{\nu_2}(\beta_2)+\cdots+\psi_{\nu_k}(\beta_k)</math> where <math>\nu_i\in\mathbb N_0, k\in\mathbb N_{>0}, \beta_i\in C_{\nu_i}(\beta_i)</math> and <math>\psi_{\nu_1}(\beta_1)\geq\psi_{\nu_2}(\beta_2)\geq\cdots\geq\psi_{\nu_k}(\beta_k)</math> and each <math> \beta_i</math> is also written in normal form.

=== Fundamental sequences ===

The fundamental sequence for an ordinal number <math>\alpha</math> with [[cofinality]] <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\beta</math> is a strictly increasing sequence <math>(\alpha[\eta])_{\eta<\beta}</math> with length <math>\beta</math> and with limit <math>\alpha</math>, where <math>\alpha[\eta]</math> is the <math>\eta</math>-th element of this sequence. If <math>\alpha</math> is a [[successor ordinal]] then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=1</math> and the fundamental sequence has only one element <math>\alpha[0]=\alpha-1</math>. If <math>\alpha</math> is a [[limit ordinal]] then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)\in\{\omega\} \cup \{\Omega_{\mu+1}\mid\mu\geq 0\}</math>.

For nonzero ordinals <math>\alpha<\Omega_\omega</math>, written in normal form, fundamental sequences are defined as follows:

#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu_1}(\beta_1)+\psi_{\nu_2}(\beta_2)+\cdots+\psi_{\nu_k}(\beta_k)</math> where <math>k\geq2</math> then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\operatorname{cof}(\psi_{\nu_k}(\beta_k))</math> and <math>\alpha[\eta]=\psi_{\nu_1}(\beta_1)+\cdots+\psi_{\nu_{k-1}}(\beta_{k-1})+(\psi_{\nu_k}(\beta_k)[\eta]),</math>
#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{0}(0)=1</math>, then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=1</math> and <math>\alpha[0]=0</math>,
#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu+1}(0)</math>, then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\Omega_{\nu+1}</math> and <math>\alpha[\eta]=\Omega_{\nu+1}[\eta]=\eta</math>,
#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu}(\beta+1)</math> then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\omega</math> and <math>\alpha[\eta]=\psi_{\nu}(\beta)\cdot \eta</math> (and note: <math>\psi_\nu(0)=\Omega_\nu</math>),
#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu}(\beta)</math> and <math>\operatorname{cof}(\beta)\in\{\omega\}\cup\{\Omega_{\mu+1}\mid\mu<\nu\}</math> then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\operatorname{cof}(\beta)</math> and <math>\alpha[\eta]=\psi_{\nu}(\beta[\eta])</math>,
#If <math>\alpha=\psi_{\nu}(\beta)</math> and <math>\operatorname{cof}(\beta)\in\{\Omega_{\mu+1}\mid\mu\geq\nu\}</math> then <math>\operatorname{cof}(\alpha)=\omega</math> and <math>\alpha[\eta]=\psi_\nu(\beta[\gamma[\eta]])</math> where <math>\left\{\begin{array}{lcr} \gamma[0]=\Omega_\mu \\ \gamma[\eta+1]=\psi_\mu(\beta[\gamma[\eta]])\\ \end{array}\right.</math>.

== Explanation ==

Buchholz is working in [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], which means every ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is equal to set <math>\{\beta\mid\beta<\alpha\}</math>. Then the condition <math>C_\nu^0(\alpha)=\Omega_\nu</math> means that set <math>C_\nu^0(\alpha)</math> includes all ordinals less than <math>\Omega_\nu</math> in other words <math>C_\nu^0(\alpha)=\{\beta\mid\beta<\Omega_\nu\}</math>.

The condition <math>C_\nu^{n+1}(\alpha) = C_\nu^n(\alpha) \cup \{\gamma \mid P(\gamma) \subseteq C_\nu^n(\alpha)\} \cup \{\psi_\mu(\xi) \mid \xi \in \alpha \cap C_\nu^n(\alpha) \wedge \mu \leq \omega\}</math> means that set <math>C_\nu^{n+1}(\alpha)</math> includes:

*all ordinals from previous set <math>C_\nu^n(\alpha)</math>,
* all ordinals that can be obtained by summation the additively principal ordinals from previous set <math>C_\nu^n(\alpha)</math>,
* all ordinals that can be obtained by applying ordinals less than <math>\alpha</math> from the previous set <math>C_\nu^n(\alpha)</math> as arguments of functions <math>\psi_\mu</math>, where <math>\mu\le\omega</math>.

That is why we can rewrite this condition as:

: <math>C_\nu^{n+1}(\alpha) = \{\beta+\gamma,\psi_\mu(\eta)\mid\beta, \gamma,\eta\in C_\nu^n(\alpha)\wedge\eta<\alpha \wedge \mu \leq \omega\}.</math>

Thus union of all sets <math>C_\nu^n (\alpha)</math> with <math>n<\omega</math> i.e. <math>C_\nu(\alpha) = \bigcup_{n < \omega} C_\nu^n (\alpha)</math> denotes the set of all ordinals which can be generated from ordinals <math><\aleph_\nu</math> by the functions + (addition) and <math>\psi_{\mu}(\eta)</math>, where <math>\mu\le\omega</math> and <math>\eta<\alpha</math>.

Then <math> \psi_\nu(\alpha) = \min\{\gamma \mid \gamma \not\in C_\nu(\alpha)\}</math> is the smallest ordinal that does not belong to this set.

'''Examples'''

Consider the following examples:

: <math>C_0^0(\alpha)=\{0\} =\{\beta\mid\beta<1\},</math>

: <math>C_0(0)=\{0\}</math> (since no functions <math>\psi(\eta<0)</math> and&nbsp;0&nbsp;+&nbsp;0&nbsp;=&nbsp;0).

Then <math>\psi_0(0)=1</math>.

<math>C_0(1)</math> includes <math>\psi_0(0)=1</math> and all possible sums of natural numbers and therefore <math>\psi_0(1)=\omega</math> – first transfinite ordinal, which is greater than all natural numbers by its definition.

<math>C_0(2)</math> includes <math>\psi_0(0)=1, \psi_0(1)=\omega</math> and all possible sums of them and therefore <math>\psi_0(2)=\omega^2</math>.

If <math>\alpha=\omega</math> then <math>C_0(\alpha)=\{0,\psi(0)=1,\ldots,\psi(1)=\omega,\ldots,\psi(2)=\omega^2,\ldots,\psi(3)=\omega^3, \ldots\}</math> and <math>\psi_0(\omega)=\omega^\omega</math>.

If <math>\alpha=\Omega</math> then <math>C_0(\alpha)=\{0,\psi(0) = 1, \ldots, \psi(1) = \omega, \ldots, \psi(\omega) = \omega^\omega, \ldots, \psi(\omega^\omega) = \omega^{\omega^\omega},\ldots\}</math> and <math>\psi_0(\Omega)=\varepsilon_0</math> – the smallest [[epsilon number]] i.e. first fixed point of <math>\alpha=\omega^\alpha</math>.

If <math>\alpha=\Omega+1</math> then <math>C_0(\alpha)=\{0,1,\ldots,\psi_0(\Omega)=\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_0+\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\psi_1(0)=\Omega,\ldots\}</math> and <math>\psi_0(\Omega+1)=\varepsilon_0\omega=\omega^{\varepsilon_0+1}</math>.

<math>\psi_0(\Omega2)=\varepsilon_1</math> the second epsilon number,

: <math>\psi_0(\Omega^2) = \varepsilon_{\varepsilon_\cdots}=\zeta_0</math> i.e. first fixed point of <math>\alpha=\varepsilon_\alpha</math>,

<math>\varphi(\alpha,\beta)=\psi_0(\Omega^\alpha(1+\beta))</math>, where <math>\varphi</math> denotes the [[Veblen function]],

<math>\psi_0(\Omega^\Omega)=\Gamma_0=\varphi(1,0,0)=\theta(\Omega,0)</math>, where <math>\theta</math> denotes the Feferman's function and <math>\Gamma_0</math> is the [[Feferman–Schütte ordinal]],

: <math>\psi_0(\Omega^{\Omega^2})=\varphi(1,0,0,0)</math> is the [[Ackermann ordinal]],

: <math>\psi_0(\Omega^{\Omega^\omega})</math> is the [[small Veblen ordinal]],

: <math>\psi_0(\Omega^{\Omega^\Omega})</math> is the [[large Veblen ordinal]],

: <math> \psi_0(\Omega\uparrow\uparrow\omega) =\psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1}) = \theta(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1},0).</math>

Now let's research how <math>\psi_1</math> works:

: <math>C_1^0(0)=\{\beta\mid\beta<\Omega_1\}=\{0,\psi(0) = 1,2, \ldots \text{googol}, \ldots, \psi_0(1)=\omega, \ldots, \psi_0(\Omega) =\varepsilon_0,\ldots</math>

<math>\ldots,\psi_0(\Omega^\Omega)=\Gamma_0,\ldots,\psi(\Omega^{\Omega^\Omega+\Omega^2}),\ldots\}</math> i.e. includes all countable ordinals. And therefore <math>C_1(0)</math> includes all possible sums of all countable ordinals and <math>\psi_1(0)=\Omega_1</math> [[first uncountable ordinal]] which is greater than all countable ordinal by its definition i.e. smallest number with cardinality <math>\aleph_1</math>.

If <math>\alpha=1</math> then <math>C_1(\alpha)=\{0,\ldots,\psi_0(0) = \omega, \ldots, \psi_1(0) = \Omega,\ldots,\Omega+\omega,\ldots,\Omega+\Omega,\ldots\}</math> and <math>\psi_1(1)=\Omega\omega=\omega^{\Omega+1}</math>.

: <math>\psi_1(2)=\Omega\omega^2=\omega^{\Omega+2},</math>

: <math>\psi_1(\psi_1(0))=\psi_1(\Omega)=\Omega^2=\omega^{\Omega+\Omega},</math>

: <math>\psi_1(\psi_1(\psi_1(0))) =\omega^{\Omega+\omega^{\Omega+\Omega}} = \omega^{\Omega\cdot\Omega} = (\omega^{\Omega})^\Omega=\Omega^\Omega,</math>

: <math>\psi_1^4(0)=\Omega^{\Omega^\Omega},</math>

: <math>\psi_1^{k+1}(0)=\Omega\uparrow\uparrow k</math> where <math>k</math> is a [[natural number]], <math>k \geq 2</math>,

: <math> \psi_1(\Omega_2) = \psi_1^\omega(0) = \Omega \uparrow\uparrow \omega = \varepsilon_{\Omega+1}.</math>

For case <math>\psi(\psi_2(0))=\psi(\Omega_2)</math> the set <math>C_0(\Omega_2)</math> includes functions <math>\psi_0</math> with all arguments less than <math>\Omega_2</math> i.e. such arguments as <math>0, \psi_1(0), \psi_1(\psi_1(0)), \psi_1^3(0),\ldots, \psi_1^\omega(0)</math>

and then

: <math> \psi_0(\Omega_2) = \psi_0(\psi_1(\Omega_2)) = \psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1}).</math>

In the general case:

: <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\nu+1}) = \psi_0(\psi_\nu(\Omega_{\nu+1})) = \psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1}) = \theta(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1},0).</math>

We also can write:

: <math>\theta(\Omega_\nu,0)=\psi_0(\Omega_\nu^\Omega) \text{ (for } 1\le\nu)<\omega</math>

== Ordinal notation ==

Buchholz<ref name="buchholz84"/> defined an [[ordinal notation]] <math>\mathsf{(OT, <)}</math> associated to the <math>\psi</math> function. We simultaneously define the sets <math>T</math> and <math>PT</math> as formal strings consisting of <math>0, D_v</math> indexed by <math>v \in \omega + 1</math>, braces and commas in the following way:

* <math>0 \in T \and 0 \in PT</math>,
* <math>\forall (v, a) \in (\omega + 1) \times T( D_va \in T \and D_va \in PT) </math>.
* <math>\forall (a_0, a_1) \in PT^2((a_0, a_1) \in T)</math>.
* <math>\exists s (a_0 = s) \and (a_0, a_1) \in T \times PT \rightarrow (s, a_1) \in T</math>.

An element of <math>T</math> is called a ''term'', and an element of <math>PT</math> is called a ''principal term''. By definition, <math>T</math> is a recursive set and <math>PT</math> is a recursive subset of <math>T</math>. Every term is either <math>0</math>, a principal term or a braced array of principal terms of length <math>\geq 2</math>. We denote <math>a \in PT</math> by <math>(a)</math>. By convention, every term can be uniquely expressed as either <math>0</math> or a braced, non-empty array of principal terms. Since clauses 3 and 4 in the definition of <math>T</math> and <math>PT</math> are applicable only to arrays of length <math>\geq 2</math>, this convention does not cause serious ambiguity. 

We then define a [[binary relation]] <math>a < b</math> on <math>T</math> in the following way:

* <math>b = 0 \rightarrow a < b = \bot</math>
* <math>a = 0 \rightarrow (a < b \leftrightarrow b \neq 0)</math>
* If <math>a \neq 0 \and b \neq 0</math>, then:
** If <math>a = D_ua' \and b = D_vb'</math> for some <math>((u, a'), (v, b')) \in ((\omega + 1) \times T)^2</math>, then <math>a < b</math> is true if either of the following are true:
*** <math>u < v</math>
*** <math>u = v \and a' < b'</math>
** If <math>a = (a_0, ..., a_n) \and b = (b_0, ..., b_m)</math> for some <math>(n, m) \in \N^2 \and 1 \leq n + m</math>, then <math>a < b</math> is true if either of the following are true:
*** <math>\forall i \in \N \and i \leq n(n < m \and a_i = b_i)</math>
*** <math>\exists k \in \N\forall i \in \N \and i < k(k \leq min\{n, m\} \and a_k < b_k \and a_i = b_1)</math>

<math><</math> is a recursive strict [[Total order|total ordering]] on <math>T</math>. We abbreviate <math>(a < b) \or (a = b)</math> as <math>a \leq b</math>. Although <math>\leq</math> itself is not a well-ordering, its restriction to a recursive subset <math>OT \subset T</math>, which will be described later, forms a well-ordering. In order to define <math>OT</math>, we define a subset <math>G_ua \subset T</math> for each <math>(u, a) \in (\omega + 1) \times T</math> in the following way:

* <math>a = 0 \rightarrow G_ua = \varnothing</math>
* Suppose that <math>a = D_va'</math> for some <math>(v, a') \in (\omega + 1) \times T</math>, then:
** <math>u \leq v \rightarrow G_ua = \{a'\} \cup G_ua'</math>
** <math>u > v \rightarrow G_ua = \varnothing</math>

* If <math>a = (a_0, ..., a_k)</math> for some <math>(a_i)_{i=0}^k \in PT^{k + 1}</math> for some <math>k \in \N \backslash \{0\}, G_ua = \bigcup_{i=0}^k G_ua_i</math>.

<math>b \in G_ua</math> is a recursive relation on <math>(u, a, b) \in (\omega + 1) \times T^2</math>. Finally, we define a subset <math>OT \subset T</math> in the following way:

* <math>0 \in OT</math>
* For any <math>(v, a) \in (\omega + 1) \times T</math>, <math>D_va \in OT</math> is equivalent to <math>a \in OT</math> and, for any <math>a' \in G_va</math>, <math>a' < a</math>.
* For any <math>(a_i)_{i=0}^k \in PT^{k + 1}</math>, <math>(a_0, ..., a_k) \in OT</math> is equivalent to <math>(a_i)_{i=0}^k \in OT</math> and <math>a_k \leq ... \leq a_0</math>.

<math>OT</math> is a recursive subset of <math>T</math>, and an element of <math>OT</math> is called an ''ordinal term''. We can then define a map <math>o: OT \rightarrow C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega+1})</math> in the following way:

* <math>a = 0 \rightarrow o(a) = 0</math>
* If <math>a = D_va'</math> for some <math>(v, a') \in (\omega + 1) \times OT</math>, then <math>o(a) = \psi_v(o(a'))</math>.
* If <math>a = (a_0, ..., a_k)</math> for some <math>(a_i)_{i=0}^k \in (OT \cap PT)^{k+1}</math> with <math>k \in \N \backslash \{0\}</math>, then <math>o(a) = o(a_0) \# ... \# o(a_k)</math>, where <math>\#</math> denotes the descending sum of ordinals, which coincides with the usual addition by the definition of <math>OT</math>.

Buchholz verified the following properties of <math>o</math>:

* The map <math>o</math> is an order-preserving bijective map with respect to <math><</math> and <math>\in</math>. In particular, <math>o</math> is a recursive strict well-ordering on <math>OT</math>.
* For any <math>a \in OT</math> satisfying <math>a < D_10</math>, <math>o(a)</math> coincides with the ordinal type of <math><</math> restricted to the countable subset <math>\{x \in OT \; | \; x < a\}</math>.
* The [[Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal]] coincides with the ordinal type of <math><</math> restricted to the recursive subset <math>\{x \in OT \; | \; x < D_10\}</math>.
* The ordinal type of <math>(OT, <)</math> is greater than the [[Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal]].
* For any <math>v \in \N \; \backslash \; \{0\}</math>, the well-foundedness of <math><</math> restricted to the recursive subset <math>\{x \in OT \; | \; x < D_0D_{v+1}0\}</math> in the sense of the non-existence of a [[Primitive recursive function|primitive recursive]] infinite descending sequence is not provable under <math>\mathsf{ID}_v</math>.
* The well-foundedness of <math><</math> restricted to the recursive subset<math>\{x \in OT \; | \; x < D_0D_\omega0\}</math> in the same sense as above is not provable under <math>\Pi^1_1 - CA_0</math>.

=== Normal form ===
The normal form for Buchholz's function can be defined by the pull-back of standard form for the ordinal notation associated to it by <math>o</math>. Namely, the set <math>NF</math> of predicates on ordinals in <math>C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math> is defined in the following way:

* The predicate <math>\alpha = _{NF}0</math> on an ordinal <math>\alpha \in C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math> defined as <math>\alpha = 0</math> belongs to <math>NF</math>.

* The predicate <math>\alpha_0 = _{NF}\psi_{k_1}(\alpha_1)</math>&nbsp;on ordinals <math>\alpha_0, \alpha_1 \in C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math>&nbsp;with <math>k_1 = \omega + 1</math>&nbsp;defined as <math>\alpha_0 = \psi_{k_1}(\alpha_1)</math>&nbsp;and <math>\alpha_1 = C_{k_1}(\alpha_1)</math>&nbsp;belongs to <math>NF</math>.
* The predicate <math>\alpha_0 = _{NF}\alpha_1 + ... + \alpha_n</math> on ordinals <math>\alpha_0, \alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n \in C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math>&nbsp;with an integer <math>n > 1</math>&nbsp;defined as <math>\alpha_0 = \alpha_1 + ... + \alpha_n</math>, <math>\alpha_1 \geq ... \geq \alpha_n</math>, and <math>\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n \in AP</math>&nbsp;belongs to <math>NF</math>. Here <math>+</math>&nbsp;is a function symbol rather than an actual addition, and <math>AP</math>&nbsp;denotes the class of additive principal numbers.

It is also useful to replace the third case by the following one obtained by combining the second condition:

* The predicate <math>\alpha_0 = _{NF}\psi_{k_1}(\alpha_1) + ... + \psi_{k_n}(\alpha_n)</math> on ordinals <math>\alpha_0, \alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n \in C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math>&nbsp;with an integer <math>n > 1</math>&nbsp;and <math>k_1, ..., k_n \in \omega + 1</math> defined as <math>\alpha_0 = \psi_{k_1}(\alpha_1) + ... + \psi_{k_n}(\alpha_n)</math>, <math>\psi_{k_1}(\alpha_1) \geq ... \geq \psi_{k_n}(\alpha_n)</math>, and <math>\alpha_1 \in C_{k_1}(\alpha_1), ..., \alpha_n \in C_{k_n}(\alpha_n) \in AP</math>&nbsp;belongs to <math>NF</math>.

We note that those two formulations are not equivalent. For example, <math>\psi_0(\Omega) + 1 = _{NF} \psi_0(\zeta_1) + \psi_0(0)</math>&nbsp;is a valid formula which is false with respect to the second formulation because of <math>\zeta_1 \neq C_0(\zeta_1)</math>, while it is a valid formula which is true with respect to the first formulation because of <math>\psi_0(\Omega) + 1 = \psi_0(\zeta_1) + \psi_0(0)</math>, <math>\psi_0(\zeta_1), \psi_0(0) \in AP</math>, and <math>\psi_0(\zeta_1) \geq \psi_0(0)</math>. In this way, the notion of normal form heavily depends on the context. In both formulations, every ordinal in <math>C_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math>&nbsp;can be uniquely expressed in normal form for Buchholz's function.

== Extension ==

This [[ordinal collapsing function]] is a sophisticated extension of Buchholz's <math>\psi</math> by mathematician Denis Maksudov. The limit of this system, sometimes called the Extended Buchholz Ordinal, is much greater, equal to <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\Omega_{\Omega_{\cdots}}})</math> where <math>\Omega_{\Omega_{\Omega_{...}}}</math> denotes the first omega fixed point. The function is defined as follows:

* Define <math>\Omega_0 = 1</math> and <math>\Omega_\nu = \aleph_\nu</math> for <math>\nu > 0</math>.
* <math>C^0_\nu(\alpha) = \{\beta \mid \beta < \Omega_\nu\}</math>
* <math>C^{n+1}_\nu(\alpha) = \{\beta + \gamma, \psi_\mu(\eta) \mid \mu, \beta, \gamma, \eta \in C^{n}_\nu(\alpha) \land \eta < \alpha\}</math>
* <math>C_\nu(\alpha) = \bigcup\limits_{n < \omega} C^n_\nu(\alpha)</math>
* <math>\psi_\nu(\alpha) = \min(\{\gamma \mid \gamma \notin C_\nu(\alpha)\})</math>
